name: כלל השרשרת לאורך מסלול – קצב שינוי טמפרטורה (באנגלית)
questiontext:
The function \(f(x,y)={{CT:0}}\), defined in the plane gives the temperature at each point \(x,y\). A particle is moving in the plane, its location at time \(t\) given by \(\alpha(t)=(x(t),y(t))=({{CT:1}},{{CT:2}}) \). Let \(g(t)\) be the function that the particle feels at time \(t\). Note that \(g(t) = f(\alpha(t))\) is a composition of two functions! Now, what is the derivative of the temperature. One way is to get an explicit formula for the function \(g(t)\) and differentiate it directly. Another way is to apply the chain rule. To do that you first have to find the derivative of both functions.

What is the temperature that the particle feels at time \(t\)?

[[input:ans1]]
[[validation:ans1]]
\(\nabla f (x,y) \) = [[input:ans2]]
[[validation:ans2]]
\(\alpha'(t)={{CT:3}}'\) = [[input:ans3]]
[[validation:ans3]]

Now use these to calculate the derivative. We recommend calculating this derivative in two different ways. First just differentiate the function \(g(t)\). Then use the chain rule:

\[\frac{dg}{dt}(t)=\nabla f(x(t),y(t))\cdot (x'(t),y'(t))\]

Make sure that the two results you obtain coincide and then enter the result in the box below. Note in your final answer \(x,y\) should no longer appear. You should just get function of a single variable \(t\)!

\(\frac{dg}{dt}(t) \)= [[input:ans4]]
[[validation:ans4]]
generalfeedback:
Outline: Compose \(f\) with the path to get \(g(t)\), then compute the two factors of the chain rule, \(\nabla f\) and \(\alpha'(t)\), and combine them; the result agrees with differentiating \(g(t)\) directly.
Step 1 — The composition
Substitute \(x=x(t)\) and \(y=y(t)\) into \(f\):

\[ g(t)=f(x(t),y(t))={{CT:4}} \]

Step 2 — The gradient of f
Differentiate \(f(x,y)={{CT:0}}\) with respect to each variable, treating the other one as a constant:

\[ f_x(x,y)={{CT:5}},\qquad f_y(x,y)={{CT:6}} \]

so

\[ \nabla f(x,y)={{CT:7}} \]

Step 3 — The velocity of the particle
Differentiate each coordinate of \(\alpha\):

\[ x'(t)={{CT:8}},\qquad y'(t)={{CT:9}},\qquad \alpha'(t)={{CT:10}} \]

Step 4 — The chain rule
Substitute \(x=x(t)\), \(y=y(t)\) into the gradient and take the dot product with \(\alpha'(t)\):

\[ \frac{dg}{dt}(t)=f_x(x(t),y(t))\,x'(t)+f_y(x(t),y(t))\,y'(t) \]

\[ =\left({{CT:11}}\right)\cdot\left({{CT:8}}\right)+\left({{CT:12}}\right)\cdot\left({{CT:9}}\right) \]

Differentiating \(g(t)\) from Step 1 directly gives the same function:

\[ \frac{dg}{dt}(t)={{CT:13}} \]

on_true.feedback: Very good, your answer for the composed function is correct.

on_false.feedback: Sorry you got the function \(g\) wrong. All you have to do here is compose the two functions \(g(t) = f(x(t),y(t)) \)

on_true.feedback: Very good, your calculation of the gradient \(\nabla f\) is correct.

on_false.feedback: No, your answer for the gradient \(\nabla f\) is wrong. Try differentiating again, and make sure that the two methods give the same result.

on_true.feedback: The derivative \(\alpha' = (x'(t),y'(t))\) you entered is correct.

on_false.feedback: Sorry, the derivative \(\alpha' = (x'(t),y'(t))\) you entered is wrong.

on_true.feedback: The derivative \(g'(t) \) you entered is correct.
